title: Does a Government Mandate Crowd Out Voluntary Corporate Social Responsibility? Evidence from India
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the implementation of a Government of India mandate that requires firms to spend at least 2% of their profits on corporate social responsibility (CSR). The results show that qualifying firms that voluntarily engaged in CSR before the mandate reduce their CSR spending afterward. Despite increasing advertisement expenditure likely to offset the lost signaling value of voluntary CSR, stock prices and operating performance of former voluntary CSR spenders who qualify under the law decline. Our results suggest that regulatory intervention in CSR can both diminish its signaling value and lead to a reduction in voluntary CSR spending.

summary.oneLiner: A CSR mandate in India led firms that previously practiced voluntary CSR to reduce spending, negatively impacting their stock performance.
summary.overview: This study examines the unintended consequences of India's mandate requiring firms to spend 2% of their profits on Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR). The authors find that companies previously committed to CSR actually cut their spending once it became a legal requirement. This suggests that the mandate stripped CSR of its value as a voluntary signal of company quality to the market. Consequently, these firms saw a decline in both their stock prices and operating performance.
summary.question: Does a government mandate requiring firms to spend a portion of profits on corporate social responsibility (CSR) crowd out pre-existing voluntary CSR efforts?
